To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Oral Rh(D)-positive and Rh(D)-negative antigens do not suppress the serum anti-Rhe(D) antibody response to intravenous challenge.

(1) oral administration of Rh antigen does not suppress the anti-Rhd antibody response; (2) oral administration of either Rhd-positive or Rhd-negative antigen can boost systemic anti-Rhd antibody in pre-sentised females; (3) oral administration of Rhd antigen does not suppress systemic antibody responses to other blood group antigens, and (4) the results do not support a role for oral Rhd antigen therapy in Rh-sensitised women.
oral administration of erythocyte membrane antigens does not suppress anti-D antibody production in humans, and can even enhance antibody responses in pre-sensitised females.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a safe and effective oral vaccine for the prevention of Rh haemolytic disease.
the immunological effects of oral administration of erythrocye membrane preparations in humans.
the development of an oral vaccine against the Rh(D) antigen, which is the most frequent cause of hemolytic disease in the newborn.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
oral Rh(D)-D negative antigen does not prevent the formation of antibodies in the Rh(D) negative individual.
oral administration of erythroid membrane antigens does not have a suppressive effect on the immune response to the Rh blood group system.
oral administration of Rh antigen is not a safe and reliable alternative to intramuscular immunization with Rh immunoglobulin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
oral immunization with red blood cell membranes, whether Rh positive or Rh negative, does not suppress the immune response to subsequent parenteral immunization with Rh-positive cells.
oral Rh antigen is not an effective treatment for Rh(D)-sensitization in pregnancy.
oral administration of erythrocyes membrane antigen does not supress anti-Rh(D)-antibody responses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oral Rh antigen does not suppress the immune response to Rh(D) in either Rh(D)-negative males, or pre-sensitized Rh-negative females.
oral administration of erythocyte membrane antigens does not suppress anti-D responses in humans.
the oral administration of Rh antigen is unlikely to be effective in the prevention of Rh immunization in Rh-sensitized women.
